segments.say: Lesson 23. Dynamic Programming: 2D (Grids & Strings). Grid paths, longest common subsequence and edit distance: filling a table cell by cell.

2D dynamic programming uses a table with rows and columns, typically for grids or for comparing two strings, where each cell is built from its neighbours. Here is an analogy. Counting routes through a city grid: the number of ways to reach a corner equals ways from the left plus ways from above. Fill the grid one cell at a time.

Why does this matter? Grid paths, longest common subsequence, edit distance (spell-check, diff tools), knapsack. A few key words. dp index r c: Answer for row r, column c (or prefixes of two strings). Prefix: The first i characters of a string. Diagonal: dp i minus 1 j minus 1: both strings shortened by one.
Unique paths (3 times 4 grid). Robot moves only right or down. The first row and first column each have exactly 1 way.
dp index r c equals dp r minus 1 c (from above) plus dp index r c minus 1 (from left) equals 1 plus 1 equals 2.
Fill row by row: 3, 4.
Last cell equals 4 plus 6 equals 10 paths. O of m, n time, and it can be done with one reusable row: O of n space.
Longest Common Subsequence: "ace" versus "abcde". dp index i j equals L C S of the first i chars of "ace" and the first j chars of "abcde". The empty-string row and column are 0.
'a' equals 'a' leads to dp equals diagonal plus 1 equals 1. Otherwise take max(up, left), which carries the 1 to the right.
Row 'c': at column 'c' they match leads to diagonal (1) plus 1 equals 2.
Row 'e': it matches at the last column, giving 2 plus 1 equals 3 ("ace"). The green cells are where matches extended the diagonal.

Two-sequence D P pattern. For two strings a and b: dp index i j equals answer for prefixes a:i and b:j. Compare the last characters:. Match leads to use dp i minus 1 j minus 1 (+1 for L C S). Mismatch leads to combine dp i minus 1 j, dp index i j minus 1, dp i minus 1 j minus 1 (max for L C S, 1 plus min for edit distance). Add an extra row and column for the empty prefix. It makes the base cases trivial.
Grid D P pattern. dp index r c depends on neighbours you've already computed (above, left). Unique paths, min path sum, obstacles (set cell equals 0), maximal square.

Other classic 2D D Ps. 0/1 Knapsack: dp index i w equals best value using the first i items within weight w. Longest palindromic subsequence / substring. Interval D P: burst balloons, matrix chain (dp over ranges i, j ).

Problem 1: Unique Paths. A robot starts at the top-left of an m times n grid and can only move right or down. How many different paths reach the bottom-right? For example, with m equals 3, n equals 7, the answer is 28.

The obvious brute force: Recursively explore every right/down path. That costs O of 2^(m+n). The smart way: dp index r c equals dp r minus 1 c plus dp index r c minus 1, with one rolling row. Step by step: Every cell in the first row or column has exactly 1 path. Then, Any other cell: paths equals paths from above plus paths from the left. Then, Fill row by row; the answer is the bottom-right cell.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of m, n time, O of n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 2: Longest Common Subsequence. Return the length of the longest common subsequence of two strings (characters in order in both, gaps allowed). For example, with text1 equals "abcde", text2 equals "ace", the answer is 3. "ace"

The obvious brute force: Generate all subsequences of one string and check each against the other. That costs O of 2 to the n, m. The smart way: Match leads to diagonal plus 1; else max(up, left). Step by step: dp index i j equals L C S of the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b. Then, If a i minus 1 equals b j minus 1: dp index i j equals dp i minus 1 j minus 1 plus 1. Then, Else: dp index i j equals max(dp i minus 1 j, dp index i j minus 1 ). Then, The answer is dp index m n.
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of m, n time, O of m, n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

Problem 3: Edit Distance. Return the minimum number of single-character edits (insert, delete, replace) needed to turn word1 into word2. For example, with "horse" leads to "ros", the answer is 3. horse leads to rorse (replace h) leads to rose (delete r) leads to ros (delete e)

The obvious brute force: Recursively try all three edits at every mismatch without caching. That costs Exponential. The smart way: Match leads to diagonal. Else 1 plus min(delete equals up, insert equals left, replace equals diagonal). Base: transforming to or from an empty string costs its length. Step by step: dp index i j equals edits to turn the first i characters of a into the first j characters of b. Then, Base cases: dp index i 0 equals i (delete all), dp index 0 j equals j (insert all). Then, Characters match leads to dp i minus 1 j minus 1. Then, Otherwise 1 plus min(delete equals up, insert equals left, replace equals diagonal).
Here is the Python solution. Complexity: O of m, n time, O of m, n space. Pause and read through it, then try writing it yourself without looking.

A likely interview question: How do you set up D P on two strings? A strong answer: dp index i j for prefixes a:i and b:j, with an extra empty row and column as base cases. Compare the last characters: match uses the diagonal, mismatch combines up, left and diagonal per the problem.
That's it for Dynamic Programming: 2D (Grids & Strings). Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
